source.title: Scalable Pre-training of Large Autoregressive Image Models
source.authors: Alaaeldin El-Nouby; Michal Klein; Shuang-Fei Zhai; Miguel Angel Bautista; Vaishaal Shankar; A. Toshev; J. Susskind; A. Joulin

record.tranche_reason: The study extends autoregressive scaling to image models and reports results for validation loss and downstream recognition. It does not reproduce or fit the original language-model scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper uses normalized pixel-level MSE as its default pre-training loss, not cross-entropy, and reports scaling trends rather than fitted power laws. Curve values reported only in figures are recorded as figure only. Cited results from other studies are not included.
record.test_reason: The study trains autoregressive image models from 0.6B to 6.5B parameters. It reports IN-1k validation loss against model size, data and FLOPs (V5), and downstream probe accuracy alongside that loss (V6). It fits no power laws and runs no extrapolation test. Loss is normalized-pixel MSE, not cross-entropy.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that AIM features improve with model capacity and data, that pre-training loss correlates with downstream performance, that there is no clear saturation up to 7B params and 2B images, and that scaling resembles LLMs. They call the FLOPs result 'consistent with Hoffmann et al.' but defer scaling-law analysis.
record.recipe_differences: This is an image-domain autoregressive transformer study using normalized pixel MSE by default, with validation loss and frozen-feature recognition evaluation. It does not apply the original language-model cross-entropy power-law fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Validation loss and downstream results vary with training dataset; the IN-1k-only run overfits, while DFN-2B+ performs best. Longer schedules reduce validation loss. The paper also reports that attentive probing and the selected feature layer affect downstream accuracy, but those findings do not test the scaling-law versions directly.

fits_no_version.finding: For AIM-0.6B, the deep vs wide architecture gives attentive-probe IN-1k accuracy 77.9 vs 78.2 (Table 3f), a small difference. The measure is downstream accuracy, not pre-training loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed parameter count, depth/width shape changes downstream probe accuracy only slightly in autoregressive image models.

record.problems: The paper reports trends rather than fitted power laws or exponents, and gives no quantified extrapolation test. Several loss results are available only as plots. The tested loss is pixel-regression MSE rather than cross-entropy, the compute-optimal allocation question is explicitly deferred, and the reported scaling evidence is limited to image models and the tested datasets and schedules.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were retained. The paper's architecture, objective, attention, and head ablations report downstream design comparisons rather than the loss-scaling or compute-allocation results in the claim versions; cited results from other studies were excluded.

untested.parts: Power-law functional form, exponents, range over several orders of magnitude; video, repeated-data, fine-tuning/transfer regimes as scaling laws.
Quantitative prediction of downstream accuracy from loss or scale; extrapolation.
No compute-optimal allocation fitted; explicitly deferred.
Depth vs width compared only on downstream accuracy, not pre-training loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or curvature.

missing.what: Validation loss per model size: 0.3119, 0.3084, 0.3039, 0.2989 (0.6B/1B/3B/7B, same updates)
IN-1k attentive-probe accuracy by size: 78.5, 80.6, 82.2, 82.4 at last layer; 79.4, 82.3, 83.3, 84.0 at best layer
LoRA fine-tuning IN-1k accuracy by size: 81.0, 83.6, 85.5, 86.3
Training length differs by model: AIM-0.6B 500k iterations, others 1.2M, which confounds Table 6 size comparisons

record.verdict_notes: No power-law fits, exponents or uncertainty are reported. The scale range is about one order of magnitude in parameters and under one in FLOPs. The headline 79.6/84.0 for AIM-7B uses layer-20 features, not the last layer. The V5 support covers trend direction only.

versions.untested_parts: The study evaluates image models, not language models, and does not test held-out language-model cross-entropy scaling.
No power laws are fitted on small runs and used to predict larger runs.
The study does not determine a loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation at fixed compute; it says further investigation is deferred.
Architecture variants are compared on downstream probing performance, not on pre-training loss at fixed parameter count as specified in this version.

The study tests image models but does not fit or report power-law exponents, establish a power-law form over several orders of magnitude, or test video, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer regimes.
The study reports correlations and monotonic performance trends, but does not quantify downstream prediction accuracy from pre-training loss or extrapolate downstream performance.
The study does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across parameter-count conventions, fitting methods, schedules, or datasets, nor test curve bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: A IM-0.6B
rows.operation_detail: Compared pre-training validation loss over training iterations across datasets.
rows.value: figure only; the text says loss falls rapidly and deteriorates at the end of training, indicating overfitting.
rows.note: The paper reports the curve and describes its direction, but gives no exact plotted value.
rows.check: This is the small-data (1M images, many epochs) arm of the data comparison. On its own it shows a data-bottlenecked overfit, which the version excludes, not a scaling effect.

rows.subject: A IM-0.6B
rows.operation_detail: Compared pre-training validation loss over training iterations across datasets.
rows.value: figure only; the text says loss starts higher and continues to decrease without signs of overfitting, converging to a point similar to IN-1k pre-training.
rows.note: The authors attribute the similar endpoint partly to distribution shift.
rows.check: Going from 1M to 2B unique images converges to a loss similar to IN-1k on IN-1k validation. The authors attribute this to distribution shift, so the benefit of more data is weak on this measure.

rows.subject: A IM-0.6B
rows.operation_detail: Compared pre-training validation loss over training iterations across datasets.
rows.value: figure only; the text says the DFN-2B and IN-1k mixture achieves the best validation-loss performance.
rows.note: DFN-2B+ is described as predominantly DFN-2B with a small amount of IN-1k data.
rows.check: The gain over DFN-2B comes from mixing in-distribution IN-1k data (p=0.2), so data scale is confounded with distribution match. It is not a clean data-scaling effect.

rows.subject: A IM models (capacity and schedule sweep)
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss as training compute increased through longer pre-training schedules and different model capacities.
rows.value: figure only; the text says longer schedules achieve significantly lower validation loss and lower-capacity models trained longer can achieve comparable loss to higher-capacity models trained shorter with similar FLOPs.
rows.note: The authors say this is consistent with Hoffmann et al. but defer investigation of the scaling-law implications.
rows.check: Directional only: loss falls with FLOPs from about 1e21 to 8e21, under one order of magnitude. The 'smaller-longer matches larger-shorter' remark bears loosely on V3, but no optimal allocation is derived.

relationships.condition: AIM image models, 0.6B–6.5B params, IN-1k validation loss, directional trend only
relationships.reason: Validation loss falls with model size (0.3119→0.2989) and with training FLOPs (R4, R9), but no power-law form is fitted.
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss decreased from 0.3119 to 0.2989 with model size and also decreased with training FLOPs, without a power-law fit.

relationships.condition: Scaling unique-image count (1M→2B) with loss measured on IN-1k validation
relationships.reason: DFN-2B converges to a loss similar to IN-1k; only adding in-distribution IN-1k data lowers it, so data scaling on this measure depends on distribution match (R2, R3).
relationships.display_finding: DFN-2B converged to loss similar to IN-1k, and only adding in-distribution IN-1k data lowered validation loss.

relationships.condition: Attentive-probe accuracy across training, model size 0.6B–3B, and pre-training datasets
relationships.reason: Downstream accuracy improves as pre-training loss improves during training (R5-R8), rises 75.6→77.6 from 0.6B to 3B (R10-R12), and its ordering across datasets matches the loss ordering (R14-R16).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy improves as pretraining loss falls, rises from 75.6 to 77.6 between 0.6B and 3B parameters, and follows the loss ordering across datasets.

relationships.reason: The 15-benchmark average rises only 77.6→77.8 (IN-1k 82.2→82.4) despite lower loss. The larger gain (to 79.6, IN-1k 84.0) needs a different probe layer, so the downstream scaling depends on layer choice (R12, R13; Table 7 in text).
relationships.display_finding: Despite lower loss, last-layer average accuracy rose only from 77.6 to 77.8 and IN-1k from 82.2 to 82.4, while changing the probe layer reached 79.6 and 84.0.

reader_labels.reason: Validation loss improves with capacity and longer training, and the paper reports continued loss decrease on DFN data; this supports scaling trends in the tested image setting, but not a fitted power-law form (R1-R4, R9).
